records.question: What is leukemia?
records.directAnswer:
Leukemia is a cancer of the blood‑forming cells that starts in the bone marrow, where blood cells are made. [S1]

It causes the marrow to produce large numbers of abnormal white blood cells that crowd out normal blood cells. [S2]

decks.text:
Leukemia arises from genetic changes in bone‑marrow cells, but the exact cause of these DNA alterations is often unknown. [S11]

The disease is classified by the type of blood cell affected (lymphocytes or myeloid cells) and whether it grows quickly (acute) or slowly (chronic). [S3] [S4]
Acute leukemias are fast‑growing and can worsen quickly without treatment, while chronic leukemias progress more slowly over many years. [S5]

Common symptoms include fatigue, fever or night sweats, easy bruising or bleeding, weight loss, and tiny red spots (petechiae) under the skin. [S6]

Chronic leukemia may not cause noticeable symptoms early on. [S7]
Treatment options depend on the leukemia type, severity, age, and overall health, and can include chemotherapy, radiation, stem‑cell transplant, and targeted therapies. [S9]

In AML, there is an increase in the number of immature white blood cells called myeloblasts (or myeloid blasts). The myeloblasts in AML are abnormal and do not become healthy white blood cells. As the number of these cells, also called leukemia cells, increases in the blood and bone marrow, there is less room for healthy platelets, red blood cells, and other white blood cells. This may lead to easy bleeding, anemia, and infection. [S14]
Risk of developing leukemia rises with age, especially after age 60, and varies by specific leukemia subtype. [S12]

records.question: What is leukemia?
records.directAnswer: Leukemia is a group of cancers that originate in the blood‑forming tissues, most commonly the bone marrow, where abnormal proliferation of white‑blood‑cell precursors crowds out normal blood cells and impairs their functions. [S1] [S3]

decks.text: Leukemia results from DNA changes in bone‑marrow cells, though the initiating causes of these mutations remain unidentified. [S12]
There are different types of leukemia. Which type of leukemia you have depends on the type of blood cell that becomes cancer and whether it grows quickly or slowly. [S6]
Common presenting features include fatigue, fever or night sweats, easy bruising or bleeding, weight loss, loss of appetite, and petechiae caused by platelet deficiency. [S7]

Treatment selection is guided by leukemia type, disease severity, patient age, and overall health, employing chemotherapy, radiation, stem‑cell transplantation, or targeted agents that attack specific cancer pathways. [S10]
In acute myeloid leukemia, accumulation of myeloblasts reduces functional red cells, platelets, and normal white cells, leading to anemia, bleeding tendencies, and infection risk. [S15]
Leukemia incidence rises with age, becoming most common after age 60, reflecting age‑related risk factors across the population. [S14]

records.question: Explain the treatment options and what affects the choice.
records.directAnswer:
Leukemia can be treated with chemotherapy, radiation therapy, chemotherapy combined with stem‑cell transplantation, or targeted therapy that attacks specific cancer cells while sparing normal tissue. [S8]

The selection of a specific treatment is guided by the leukemia type (acute versus chronic, lymphoid versus myeloid), disease severity, the patient’s age, and overall health status. [S8]

records.question: I have a sore throat. What can cause it and do antibiotics help?
records.directAnswer:
A sore throat can be caused by many things, most often a viral cold or flu, but also allergies, mononucleosis, smoking, strep throat, or tonsillitis. [S2]

Antibiotics only help when the sore throat is due to a bacterial infection like strep throat; they do not help viral causes. [S7] [S9]

decks.text: Common causes of sore throat include colds, flu, allergies, mononucleosis, smoking, strep throat, and tonsillitis. [S2]
Most sore throats improve on their own within about one week. [S4]

Seek medical care if you have difficulty breathing or swallowing, blood in saliva, excessive drooling, dehydration, joint pain, rash, or worsening symptoms. [S5]

General guidance advises seeing a provider for severe or concerning sore throat symptoms. [S6]

Supportive care such as lozenges, fluids, gargling, and over‑the‑counter pain relievers can ease throat pain. [S3]

Antibiotics are useful for strep throat and can speed recovery, but they are ineffective for viral sore throats. [S7] [S9]
If strep throat is not treated, it can lead to complications like abscesses, ear infections, kidney inflammation, rheumatic fever, or sinus infections. [S10]
Prevent sore throats by washing hands, avoiding close contact with sick people, and not smoking or exposing yourself to secondhand smoke. [S8]

records.question: I have a sore throat. What can cause it and do antibiotics help?
records.directAnswer: If the sore throat is viral, antibiotics do not provide benefit, and most cases improve within one week without antimicrobial therapy. [S7]

decks.text: You can have a sore throat for many reasons. Often, colds and flu cause sore throats. Other causes can include: • Allergies • Mononucleosis • Smoking • Strep throat • Tonsillitis [S2]
Most sore throats improve on their own within one week. [S4]
Seek care for severe symptoms such as difficulty breathing, swallowing, blood in saliva, excessive drooling, dehydration, joint pain, rash, or lack of improvement. [S5]

Supportive care includes lozenges, fluids, gargling, and over‑the‑counter analgesics; aspirin is avoided in children. [S3]

Antibiotics are ineffective for viral sore throats but are indicated for confirmed streptococcal infection. [S7] [S9]
Untreated streptococcal infection can lead to abscesses, ear infections, glomerulonephritis, rheumatic fever, or sinus infections. [S10]
Hand hygiene, avoiding close contact with infected individuals, and not smoking reduce the risk of sore throat. [S8]

records.question: When should someone seek medical care for a sore throat?
records.directAnswer:
Seek medical care if you have difficulty breathing or swallowing, notice blood in your saliva, drool excessively, become dehydrated, develop joint pain, rash, or if symptoms worsen or do not improve after a few days. [S5]

General guidance also recommends seeing a provider for any severe or concerning sore‑throat symptoms, including recurrent episodes. [S6]

records.question: When should someone seek medical care for a sore throat?
